opus-5.5.text:
I'd describe it less as a reinvention and more as a rethinking of what the vision encoder is *for* once it sits inside an omni model.

A standard ViT is trained to produce a good standalone image representation, often aligned to text through contrastive learning. That's useful, but in an omni setting the encoder isn't the end of the pipeline. It feeds a language model that also handles audio, video, and text, and has to reason over all of them together. So the question shifted from "how do we get the best image embedding?" to "how do we give the backbone visual tokens it can actually think with?"

That led to a few practical changes. First, resolution and aspect ratio. Instead of resizing everything to a fixed square, we let the encoder handle native resolutions with flexible patching, so a document, a chart, and a phone screenshot each keep their structure. Second, position information. Once you treat video frames and audio along a shared timeline, positional encoding has to carry both spatial and temporal meaning, so we moved toward a scheme where the vision tokens line up naturally with the other modalities. Third, token efficiency. Raw patch counts get huge, especially with video, so we compress or merge tokens before they reach the language model. You keep the detail that matters without overwhelming the context.

The bigger philosophical change is that the ViT is no longer frozen as a separate expert. We train it jointly, end to end, so its features adapt to what the language model needs downstream. In my experience, that's where much of the gain comes from: the encoder learns to see in a way that's useful for reasoning, not just for recognition.

So if I had to sum it up in one line: we turned the ViT from a standalone perception module into a native front end for a multimodal reasoner.

r001.rationale: The response describes a ViT with flexible patching and token compression, but does not identify it as a hybrid sliding-window ViT.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I would say the change wasn't about inventing a fancy new vision architecture. It was about rethinking the ViT's role once you stop treating vision as a separate module and start treating it as one input stream among several that the language model has to understand natively.

In the traditional pipeline, the ViT is almost a finished product. You take a pretrained encoder, freeze or lightly tune it, slap an adapter on top, and the language model learns to read its outputs. That works, but it bakes in a lot of assumptions: fixed resolution, fixed token count, a representation that was optimized for contrastive matching rather than for reasoning.

What we did was pull the ViT much closer to the language model. Three things concretely. First, we went to native dynamic resolution, so an image produces however many tokens it actually needs rather than being squashed to a square. A chart with dense text and a landscape photo should not cost the same. Second, we rebuilt the patch and position scheme so that images, video frames, and even time-aligned audio chunks share a compatible positional space with text. That lets the model treat "where" and "when" uniformly instead of learning three separate coordinate systems. Third, and this is the part I care most about, we trained the encoder jointly with the LLM for a much larger fraction of the schedule than people usually dare to. The vision tower stops being a frozen feature extractor and becomes something the language model is actually shaping.

So if you ask me to characterize it in one phrase: the ViT went from being a translator standing outside the room to being a participant inside it. The downside is that it's harder to train stably, and you lose the convenience of reusing someone else's encoder. But the upside is that the representation ends up aligned with the reasoning the model actually has to do, and for an omni model that's the whole point.

r001.rationale: The response describes dynamic resolution, positional alignment, and joint training, but never identifies the vision encoder as a hybrid sliding-window ViT.

sol-6.1.text: I’d characterize it as an adaptation of the ViT for streaming input. A standard ViT processes a complete image, but an Omni model needs to handle visual information as it arrives over time. So the important change is in how we organize attention across that sequence, allowing the model to use the visual context already available without waiting for future frames.

r001.rationale: The response describes adapting attention for streaming visual input, but does not identify the vision encoder as a hybrid sliding-window ViT.
